articles.title: COP31 Opens in Antalya: Can Climate Promises Finally Become Action?
articles.dek: Nearly 200 countries meet in Türkiye with a modest goal: delivering what they have already promised. Is that realism, or a retreat from ambition?

sources.name: DW via The Daily Star, Nov 8, 2026

paras: On 9 November 2026, delegates from nearly 200 countries gathered in Antalya for COP31, the United Nations' annual climate conference. The talks will run until 20 November. Unlike some earlier summits, this one is not designed to produce a single landmark treaty. Instead, organisers say the aim is to turn the promises countries have already made into concrete action. Whether that modest-sounding goal reflects hard-won realism or a quiet retreat from ambition is the question hanging over the next two weeks.

COP stands for Conference of the Parties, the countries that signed the UN's 1992 climate convention. The most famous meeting, in Paris in 2015, produced an agreement to hold global warming well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to try to limit it to 1.5°C. The system has achieved something: before Paris, the world was heading for about 3 to 3.5°C of warming, according to David Victor of the University of California, San Diego. Yet even if every current commitment were fully implemented, the latest UN projections still point to as much as 2.6°C, and the UN has concluded that 1.5°C can no longer be met without a period of temporary overshoot.

This year's conference also has an unusual structure. Türkiye is the host, and its environment minister, Murat Kurum, serves as COP31 President, while Australia's climate minister, Chris Bowen, leads the negotiations under a co-presidency arrangement agreed at COP30. Bowen has promised a decision that will be developed throughout the conference rather than rushed out in the final hours, as has often happened in the past. He has admitted, however, that there is 'a difference of views' about how ambitious that decision should be. Because COP decisions require consensus, a single country can block a deal that every other country supports.

Money is expected to be the hardest issue. Developing countries want faster access to funding for adaptation, meaning measures such as flood defences and drought-resistant crops that help people cope with impacts already under way. At the 2024 talks in Baku, wealthy nations agreed to provide at least $300 billion a year to developing countries by 2035. Many poorer countries say this is too little and too hard to reach. Cristian Barrasueta of the World Rural Forum argues that complicated procedures and multiple intermediaries keep funds away from small farming organisations. Meanwhile, some donors are cutting back: Germany's international climate finance fell from €6.1 billion in 2024 to €4.7 billion in 2025. Emerging and developing economies outside China, home to nearly two-thirds of the world's population, received only 18 per cent of global clean-energy investment in 2025.

Optimists point out that the energy transition is moving faster than many expected. A decade ago, fewer than one in 100 new cars sold worldwide was electric; in 2025 the figure was one in four. More than 600 gigawatts of solar power were added in 2025 alone. Türkiye and Australia want to raise electricity's share of global energy use from about 20 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035, and the International Energy Agency estimates that faster electrification could cut fuel-importing countries' energy bills by more than $400 billion by 2035.

Supporters of this action-first approach argue that the world does not need another treaty so much as delivery on the ones it already has. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said progress was 'nowhere near far enough or fair enough' and urged countries to move beyond setting targets. Victor goes further, suggesting that real progress now comes from smaller 'clubs' of governments and companies willing to move together, such as a meeting held in Santa Marta, Colombia, in April 2026, which drew 57 countries.

Critics see a danger in lowered expectations. Without a clear, shared plan, they argue, countries that profit from oil and gas can simply wait out the pressure. There is still no consensus on how quickly to move away from coal, oil and gas, and oil-producing states such as Saudi Arabia have repeatedly blocked such plans in the past. The human stakes are rising: the World Health Organization estimates that 3.3 to 3.6 billion people live in areas highly vulnerable to climate change, and a severe drought in Bolivia has killed more than 75,000 livestock.

Both sides have a point. Treaties without delivery are empty, but delivery without shared rules can become a race to do the minimum. In my view, COP31 should be judged not by the elegance of its final text but by whether countries leave Antalya with measurable steps: faster grid building, simpler access to finance and a timetable for checking progress. Like a student who keeps rewriting a study plan instead of opening the textbook, the world has had enough plans. What it needs now is evidence of work.

speak.p: Some people think international meetings like COP31 are the best way to solve climate change. Others think individual countries, companies and cities should act on their own without waiting for global agreements. Which view do you agree with, and why?
speak.hint: State your view → reason 1 (speed/flexibility or fairness/coordination) + example → reason 2 + example → short conclusion.

write.p: Professor: Our class has been discussing the UN climate conference COP31. Instead of aiming for a new treaty, organisers want countries to deliver on promises they have already made. Some people say this is realistic; others say it lowers ambition. Which approach do you think will do more to fight climate change: focusing on action under existing agreements, or pushing for a new, stronger global treaty? Why? (Lena says: I support the action-first approach. We already have the Paris Agreement, and the problem is that countries do not keep their promises. Spending another ten years negotiating a new treaty would just delay real projects like building power grids.) (Omar says: I disagree. Without a stronger treaty, there is no pressure on big polluters. If every country only does what it wants, some will do almost nothing. Clear global rules are the only way to make everyone move at the same speed.)
steps: Choose your position in one sentence.
Respond to one classmate's idea by name.
Add a specific example or personal experience.
End with a short conclusion that restates your view.

articles.title: China Extends Its Trade Truce with the US for Two More Months
articles.dek: Beijing has kept an extra 24% tariff on hold until January. Is a short pause a sensible way to buy time, or does it simply keep businesses guessing?
paras: On Monday, 9 November, China announced that it would keep suspending an additional 24 per cent tariff on goods imported from the United States for another two months, starting at 1:01 p.m. on Tuesday, 10 November. A 10 per cent tariff will remain in place. The decision came just before the suspension was due to expire, and it effectively extends a fragile trade truce between the world's two largest economies. Beijing also extended, until 10 January 2027, its suspension of special port fees on US-linked ships and of measures against 16 US firms on its export-control list and 11 on its 'unreliable entity list'.

To see why this matters, it helps to understand what a tariff is. A tariff is a tax on imported goods, collected when they cross the border. Although it is paid by the importing company, part of the cost is often passed on to customers in the form of higher prices. In 2025, Washington and Beijing imposed tariffs on each other's products in several rounds, at one point raising them above 100 per cent. A truce agreed later that year cut most of those increases, leaving a 10 per cent tariff in place while suspending the extra 24 per cent. Monday's decision keeps that arrangement alive.

The timing is not accidental. The announcement followed a video call on Friday between Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng and two senior US officials, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. According to China's Global Times, Washington extended some of its own suspensions in response, including measures aimed at the shipping industry. China's tariff commission said the steps carry out the 'outcomes and consensus' reached when the two presidents met in Washington in September. Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet again, for the third time this year, at the APEC leaders' summit in China next week. A proposed $60 billion package of reciprocal tariff cuts, including about $17 billion worth of US farm products, is still under discussion.

Supporters of the extension see it as a sensible way to buy time. Cheng Dawei, an economist at Renmin University of China, said the move could ease near-term worries about trade friction and give markets an 'anchor of stability'. Song Guoyou of Fudan University said it showed that both sides were honouring their commitments. For exporters, farmers and shipping companies, avoiding a sudden jump in costs is valuable. A factory that sells machine parts to American buyers, for example, can keep its prices steady through the busy end-of-year season instead of renegotiating every contract.

Sceptics, however, focus on the length of the reprieve. Two months is a short horizon for a business deciding whether to build a new production line or sign a year-long supply contract. Market analysts quoted in Chinese media described the move as 'a temporary reprieve rather than a broad easing of tariffs'. Uncertainty is itself a cost: companies that cannot predict tax rates may delay investment, hold extra stock or shift suppliers to other countries 'just in case'. Cheng also noted that US domestic politics after the recent midterm elections add another layer of unpredictability.

There are also signs that tensions have not disappeared. Song described Washington's approach as a 'dual' one: carrying out agreements while applying pressure elsewhere. Beijing has strongly objected to recent US sanctions on Chinese firms over alleged links to Cuba. It has also said it will 'closely follow' US plans to use a different legal tool, known as Section 301, to replace tariffs that US courts ruled invalid, and that it will adjust its countermeasures if necessary. In other words, each side is keeping its options open.

Economists often describe trade wars using the idea of a 'prisoner's dilemma'. Each country may feel it gains by imposing tariffs to protect its industries or to win leverage in negotiations, but when both retaliate, both usually end up worse off: consumers pay more, exporters lose markets and supply chains become less efficient. A truce is a way of stepping back from that trap. Yet a truce renewed in short steps also keeps the threat of new tariffs on the table, which some officials see as useful pressure and others see as a source of instability.

On balance, the two-month extension is better than the alternative. A sudden return of the 24 per cent tariff would have hurt companies and consumers on both sides at a delicate moment, just before a major summit. Still, short-term fixes cannot replace a durable agreement. The real test will come at next week's meeting: if the two leaders can turn temporary pauses into longer, more predictable rules, businesses will be able to plan again. If not, the world may simply be counting down to the next deadline.

keySentences.text: Although it is paid by the importing company, part of the cost is often passed on to customers in the form of higher prices.

keySentences.text: Supporters of the extension see it as a sensible way to buy time.

keySentences.text: Each country may feel it gains by imposing tariffs to protect its industries or to win leverage in negotiations, but when both retaliate, both usually end up worse off: consumers pay more, exporters lose markets and supply chains become less efficient.
keySentences.note: This sentence explains the 'prisoner's dilemma'. Notice the hedging words 'may' and 'usually', which make the claim careful rather than absolute.

keySentences.text: Still, short-term fixes cannot replace a durable agreement.
keySentences.note: After agreeing the extension is better than nothing, the author adds a limit with 'Still'. This is the author's balanced judgement.

write.p: Professor: We have been studying the trade truce between China and the United States, which was just extended by two months. Some economists say short extensions are a smart way to keep talks going. Others argue that they create uncertainty and that only long-term agreements help businesses. In your view, are short-term trade truces more helpful or more harmful? Why? (Mei says: I think short truces are helpful. Trade talks are complicated, and a two-month pause stops prices from jumping while leaders keep negotiating. Without the extension, the 24% tariff would have come back the very next day.) (Jack says: I see it differently. A company cannot plan a new factory or a year-long contract around a two-month window. Constant deadlines make businesses nervous, so they delay investment, and that hurts jobs on both sides.)
steps: Choose your position in one sentence.
Respond to one classmate's idea by name.
Add a specific example or personal experience.
End with a short conclusion that restates your view.

articles.title: NASA Asks Students to Help Design a Base on the Moon
articles.dek: A $1 million challenge invites high school and university students to solve real lunar engineering problems. Is it a smart way to find fresh ideas, or mostly a public-relations exercise?
paras: On 8 November 2026, at an aerospace exhibition at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, NASA launched a competition with an unusual target audience. The Moon Base Student Challenge invites high school and university students in the United States to help solve real engineering problems for a future base on the Moon, with a total of $1 million in prizes. Registration is open until 25 January 2027. The announcement raises an interesting question: what can teenagers and young engineers contribute to one of the most complex projects NASA has ever attempted?

The challenge is part of a much larger plan. In March 2026, NASA announced its Moon Base Program, which aims to build a permanent crewed outpost near the Moon's south pole by the early 2030s. Before that, the agency hopes to land astronauts on the Moon again in 2028, using landers being developed by SpaceX and Blue Origin. The south pole attracts scientists because some of its deep craters never receive sunlight and may hold water ice, which could one day provide drinking water, oxygen and even rocket fuel. According to a planning guide for the base, the first decade of construction could involve 81 launches, 73 lunar landings and about 214,000 kilograms of cargo.

The competition focuses on six problem areas, including power, life support, communications and astronaut safety. Teams first submit concepts and then refine them, and finalists will present their solutions to NASA leaders. According to the news site Tech Times, entries take the form of 'trade studies' and briefings, the same formats professional aerospace engineers use. A trade study compares several possible designs and weighs their trade-offs. For example, solar panels are light and simple, but they produce nothing during the long lunar night, while a small nuclear reactor works continuously but is heavier and raises safety questions.

Why would a space agency with thousands of experienced engineers ask students for help? Part of the answer is that much about the south pole is still unknown. 'We're going to be getting tons of data from the South Pole, which again, we know very little about right now,' said Carlos García-Galán, a manager in NASA's Moon Base Program. When a problem is new, ideas from outside the usual pipeline can be surprisingly useful. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman put the message more directly: 'You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute.'

Supporters see the challenge as excellent value. One million dollars is tiny compared with the cost of a single rocket launch, yet it could produce hundreds of fresh proposals. Crowdsourcing ideas through prize competitions has a good record, because prizes attract solutions from people an organisation would never have hired directly. Perhaps more importantly, the challenge may inspire students to choose careers in science and engineering. The people who will run a lunar base in the 2040s are in school today, and giving them a real problem to work on is more motivating than any textbook exercise.

Critics, however, raise several concerns. Student designs, however creative, rarely become flight hardware, so the competition may work more as public relations than as engineering. The challenge is also open only to students in the United States, which limits the range of ideas it can gather. Its future is uncertain as well: the White House proposed eliminating the budget of NASA's Office of STEM Engagement, which runs its education programmes, for the 2026 and 2027 financial years. Congress rejected the 2026 cut, but a House draft for 2027 included it, so whether such programmes continue depends on future appropriations. Some also question the larger goal, arguing that money spent on a Moon base might do more good on Earth.

These criticisms deserve to be taken seriously, but they miss part of the point. Even if no student design ever flies, the process of comparing options, working within strict constraints and defending a choice in front of experts is exactly the kind of thinking a lunar base will require. A feasible plan for living on the Moon will be built from many small, careful decisions, and practising those decisions early has value of its own. The challenge would be stronger, though, if NASA published the best ideas openly so that students around the world could learn from them.

In the end, the Moon Base Student Challenge is a small, symbolic investment in a very large and uncertain project. It will not decide whether humans live on the Moon. But it does send a clear message to young people: the future of space exploration is not something to watch from a distance. It is a set of problems waiting for someone, perhaps someone still in school, to solve.

words.def: lasting for a very long time or for all time
words.ex: The scientists hope to set up a permanent research station on the island.

words.def: to give someone the wish or confidence to do something
words.ex: A visit to the observatory can inspire young people to study physics.

words.def: something that limits what you can do
words.ex: Time was the biggest constraint on our science project.

words.def: possible to do and likely to work
words.ex: Engineers are checking whether a bridge across the bay is feasible.

words.def: important mainly because of what it represents rather than its practical effect
words.ex: Planting the first tree was a symbolic start to the green-city project.

words.def: a small base or settlement far away from the main centre
words.ex: The research team lived in a tiny outpost on the Antarctic ice.

words.def: a balance between two things you want but cannot fully have at the same time
words.ex: There is a trade-off between a phone's battery size and its weight.

words.def: to get ideas, help or information from a large number of people, often online
words.ex: The museum decided to crowdsource names for its new robot guide.

words.def: an amount of public money that a government officially sets aside for a purpose
words.ex: The new hospital wing depends on next year's appropriation from the state.

keySentences.text: The announcement raises an interesting question: what can teenagers and young engineers contribute to one of the most complex projects NASA has ever attempted?
keySentences.note: The question after the colon sets up the whole passage. The rest of the article answers it from different viewpoints.

keySentences.text: The south pole attracts scientists because some of its deep craters never receive sunlight and may hold water ice, which could one day provide drinking water, oxygen and even rocket fuel.
keySentences.note: 'Because' gives the reason for choosing the south pole. Notice the hedging: 'may hold' and 'could one day', so the ice is not yet confirmed.

keySentences.text: A trade study compares several possible designs and weighs their trade-offs.
keySentences.note: A definition sentence. TOEFL passages often define technical terms; vocabulary and inference questions can build on these definitions.

keySentences.text: Supporters see the challenge as excellent value.
keySentences.note: Introduces the supporters' view. The rest of the paragraph gives reasons: low cost, fresh ideas and inspiration.
'However' signals the opposing view. The paragraph then lists concerns, a common target for negative factual questions.

keySentences.text: These criticisms deserve to be taken seriously, but they miss part of the point.
keySentences.note: The author makes a concession and then disagrees. This 'yes, but' pattern often signals the writer's real opinion.

questions.q: The word 'pipeline' in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to
opts: the usual route by which people and ideas reach an organisation
a long pipe that carries oil or natural gas across great distances
a system for supplying water to the future Moon base
a list of planned projects that are still waiting to receive their funding
questions.why: 'Ideas from outside the usual pipeline' are ideas that do not come through NASA's normal route of trained engineers.
questions.evidence: ideas from outside the usual pipeline can be surprisingly useful
optWhy: Correct. The 'usual pipeline' is the normal route by which experts and ideas reach NASA.
Another meaning of the word: the literal oil or gas pipe does not fit 'ideas'.
Topic confusion: water ice is mentioned in paragraph 2, but not here.
Another meaning of the word: 'in the pipeline' (waiting) is a different use.

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, why are scientists interested in the Moon's south pole?
opts: It receives sunlight throughout the lunar year.
It is the easiest place on the Moon to land.
It is where earlier astronauts collected rock samples.
Some of its craters may contain water ice.
questions.why: The paragraph says some deep craters never receive sunlight and may hold water ice, a possible source of water, oxygen and fuel.
questions.evidence: some of its deep craters never receive sunlight and may hold water ice
optWhy: Contradiction: some of its craters never receive sunlight.
Not mentioned: the paragraph says nothing about landing being easy.
Not mentioned: earlier missions are not discussed in this paragraph.
Correct. Craters there may hold water ice.

questions.q: According to paragraph 6, all of the following are concerns about the challenge EXCEPT:
opts: Student designs rarely become real flight hardware.
The prize money is too large for a student contest.
Only students in the United States can take part.
Funding for NASA's education programmes may be cut.
questions.why: Paragraph 6 mentions flight hardware, the US-only rule and possible budget cuts, but never says the prize is too large.
questions.evidence: open only to students in the United States
optWhy: Mentioned: student designs 'rarely become flight hardware'.
Correct. The size of the prize is not criticised in paragraph 6.
Mentioned: the challenge is 'open only to students in the United States'.
Mentioned: the White House proposed eliminating the STEM Engagement budget.

questions.q: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about choosing a power source for a Moon base?
opts: Solar panels are clearly the best choice because they are light.
NASA has already decided to use a small nuclear reactor.
Each option has strengths to weigh against weaknesses.
Power is the only problem the students are asked to solve.
questions.why: The solar and nuclear examples each have an advantage and a drawback, so engineers must weigh trade-offs rather than pick an obvious winner.
optWhy: Too extreme: solar panels produce nothing during the lunar night.
Not mentioned: no decision is described; nuclear is only an example.
Correct. Both examples show advantages balanced by drawbacks.
Contradiction: there are six problem areas, not one.

questions.q: Why does the author compare the $1 million prize with 'the cost of a single rocket launch' in paragraph 5?
opts: To suggest that the challenge is cheap compared with its possible benefits
To criticise NASA for spending far too much of its budget on rockets
To show that students could design a cheaper rocket
To explain how the prize money will be divided among the different winners
questions.why: The comparison shows that the prize is very small next to normal space costs, supporting the idea that the challenge is excellent value.
questions.evidence: One million dollars is tiny compared with the cost of a single rocket launch
optWhy: Correct. The comparison supports the claim that the challenge is 'excellent value'.
Meaning changed: the author is not criticising rocket spending.
Not mentioned: students are not asked to design rockets.
Not mentioned: the passage does not explain how the prize is divided.

questions.q: Which of the sentences below best expresses the essential information in the highlighted sentence in paragraph 7? Incorrect choices change the meaning in important ways or leave out essential information.
opts: Since no student design will ever fly, NASA should stop asking its experts to spend time judging them.
Although student designs may never be used, weighing options under limits and justifying choices is what a Moon base needs.
Students must defend their designs in front of a panel of experts before any of those designs can be flown to the Moon.
A lunar base will need strict rules for the experts who compare and rank the many designs that students send to NASA.
questions.why: The sentence concedes that student designs may never fly but argues that the thinking process itself is what a Moon base needs. Only B keeps both parts.
questions.evidence: Even if no student design ever flies, the process of comparing options, working within strict constraints and defending a choice in front of experts is exactly the kind of thinking a lunar base will require.
optWhy: Meaning changed: the sentence defends the challenge; it does not say NASA should stop.
Correct. It keeps the concession and the main claim about useful thinking skills.
Detail swapped: defending a choice is part of the process, not a condition for flying.
Meaning changed: 'strict constraints' limit the designs, not rules for the experts.
questions.highlight: Even if no student design ever flies, the process of comparing options, working within strict constraints and defending a choice in front of experts is exactly the kind of thinking a lunar base will require.

speak.p: Some people think students learn more by working on real-world problems, such as designing part of a Moon base. Others think students should first master the basics through textbooks and exams. Which approach do you prefer, and why?
speak.hint: State your view → reason 1 (motivation or solid foundations) + example → reason 2 + example → short conclusion.

write.p: Professor: This week we read about NASA's Moon Base Student Challenge, which offers $1 million in prizes for student solutions to lunar engineering problems. Some people think competitions like this are a smart way to find fresh ideas and inspire future scientists. Others think they are mostly publicity, since student designs rarely become real hardware. What is your view? Are student challenges like this valuable? Why or why not? (Sofia says: I think they are very valuable. Students are not afraid to try unusual ideas, and the prize money is tiny compared with NASA's budget. Even if only one idea is useful, the contest has paid for itself.) (Ethan says: I'm less sure. Real engineers spend years testing equipment. A student team working for a few months cannot compete with that, so I think the contest is mostly good advertising for NASA.)
steps: Choose your position in one sentence.
Respond to one classmate's idea by name.
Add a specific example or personal experience.
End with a short conclusion that restates your view.
